prompt.context: A medical equipment manufacturer in the southeastern U.S. has called you in because it feels its working capital requirements are much higher than those of its competitors.
prompt.question: How will you help it solve its problem?

clarifying_info.q: What makes up the company's current assets and current liabilities?
clarifying_info.a: Current assets consist of cash, inventory, and accounts receivable. Current liabilities consist of accounts payable and short-term debts.

clarifying_info.q: Can you tell me more about the company's structure or background?
clarifying_info.a: The company is made up of three divisions. The high inventory problem can be traced to a division acquired about two years ago. That division manufactures equipment for arthroscopic surgery — capital equipment and blades — similar to a razor/razor-blade model, just much more sophisticated and expensive.

clarifying_info.q: Why might inventory levels be so high?
clarifying_info.a: Technology has been changing rapidly and the rate of obsolescence is extremely high. Earlier sales forecasts (made shortly after the acquisition) were overly optimistic, leaving the client with a large stock of obsolescent finished goods inventory.

framework: Anchor on Working Capital = Current Assets minus Current Liabilities
Break down Current Assets: cash, inventory, accounts receivable — identify which is inflated
Break down Current Liabilities: accounts payable, short-term debt — assess payment terms
Hypothesize root causes for elevated working capital vs. competitors: high inventory, slow AR collection, or low AP leverage
Zero in on Inventory as the primary driver given the acquisition context
Explore why inventory is high: over-forecasted demand, rapid technology obsolescence, poor inventory management

questions.prompt: What are the possible reasons for the company's inventory being excessively high?
questions.guidance: A strong answer covers three buckets: (1) demand/sales forecasting — projections were too optimistic post-acquisition; (2) poor forecasting processes — lack of rolling forecast discipline; (3) technology obsolescence — rapid product-technology change has rendered finished goods outdated. The candidate should also mention the razor/razor-blade nature of the product line (capital equipment + blades) and how that affects inventory dynamics.

questions.prompt: The client has 2.5 years of capital equipment finished goods inventory, and NONE of it needs to be carried because these items can now be manufactured only after receiving an order (the finished-good product is no longer sold). What are the next steps?
questions.guidance: An ideal answer addresses three avenues: (1) Salvage/Dismantle — strip the obsolescent units for reusable component parts to incorporate into new devices; (2) Liquidate — sell off inventory to distributors in less technologically advanced healthcare markets where the older product still has value; (3) Write-off — recognize a write-down/write-off on non-salvageable components. The candidate should also recommend forward-looking corrective actions: institute demand-driven (make-to-order) manufacturing for capital equipment, tighten sales forecasting discipline, and set target inventory days in line with competitors.

brainstorming.prompt: What corrective actions should the client take to reduce its working capital and bring inventory to an appropriate level?

categories.name: Inventory Reduction
ideas: Dismantle obsolescent capital equipment and reuse salvageable component parts
Sell excess inventory to distributors in less advanced healthcare markets
Write off non-salvageable finished goods and components
Switch capital equipment manufacturing to a make-to-order model (no finished goods stock required)

categories.name: Demand Forecasting Improvement
ideas: Implement rolling sales forecasts reviewed monthly
Align sales incentives with forecast accuracy
Use historical sell-through data and market intelligence rather than post-acquisition growth assumptions

categories.name: Inventory Policy
ideas: Set target days-of-inventory benchmarked against competitors
Define safety stock levels based on actual lead times and customer order lead times
Establish an obsolescence review process tied to product life-cycle milestones

categories.name: Accounts Receivable
ideas: Review collection terms and tighten DSO
Offer early-payment discounts to key customers

categories.name: Accounts Payable
ideas: Negotiate extended payment terms with suppliers
Align payables cycle with receivables cycle to reduce net working capital

recommendation: Immediately take action on the 2.5-year capital equipment inventory: dismantle for salvageable parts, sell remainder to less-advanced markets, and write off what cannot be recovered
Shift capital equipment manufacturing to a make-to-order model, eliminating the need to carry finished goods
Implement a rigorous, rolling demand-forecasting process with accountability tied to sales and operations planning
risks: Write-offs will impact the P&L and may require explanation to investors/leadership
Selling to less-advanced markets at discount erodes margins
Make-to-order transition requires reliable manufacturing lead times — customer expectations must be managed
next_steps: Conduct a physical inventory audit to classify each SKU as salvageable, sellable, or write-off
Benchmark working capital ratios (inventory days, DSO, DPO) against direct competitors to quantify the gap
Build a 90-day action plan with milestones for inventory reduction and process changes
Establish ongoing KPI dashboards for inventory days and working capital as a percentage of revenue
